title: THE BIBLE NAMES WOMEN WHO WERE CONCUBINES—BUT NEVER TELLS US IF THEY HAD A CHOICE. AND THAT SILENCE SHOULD BREAK OUR HEARTS.
paragraphs: THE BIBLE NAMES WOMEN WHO WERE CONCUBINES—BUT NEVER TELLS US IF THEY HAD A CHOICE. AND THAT SILENCE SHOULD BREAK OUR HEARTS.

They lived in the households of powerful men. Their bodies became part of royal histories. Their suffering was sometimes recorded in a single sentence. But beneath the silence of Scripture is a truth we cannot afford to miss: God sees the people history treats as disposable—and Jesus came to redeem a world that learned to look away.
There is something deeply unsettling about reading the Bible slowly.
Not because Scripture is untrustworthy.
But because sometimes, when you stop rushing past the familiar names, you discover someone standing in the background of a story you thought you already understood.
A woman.
Sometimes named. Sometimes unnamed.
Sometimes introduced as a concubine, then mentioned only when something terrible happens to her.
And then the narrative moves on.
Kings continue ruling. Families continue fighting. Nations continue rising and falling.
But what happened to her?
Did she have a mother who missed her?
Did she ever dream of having a home where she was loved rather than possessed?
Did she have a choice?
And perhaps the most painful question of all...
How many times have we read her story without even noticing that she was there?
Before we go any further, we need to understand something essential.
The Bible's record of an event is not automatically God's approval of that event.
Scripture tells us about betrayal, murder, exploitation, polygamy, sexual violence, and the abuse of power. But describing what human beings did is not the same as commanding us to imitate them.
In fact, some of the Bible's most disturbing narratives expose just how far humanity had wandered from God's design.
And when we encounter the women called concubines, we must resist two temptations.
We must not romanticize their circumstances.
And we must not invent details about their lives that Scripture never reveals.
Because honoring their humanity requires telling the truth—even when the truth is that we do not know.
In biblical Hebrew, one word translated as "concubine" is פִּילֶגֶשׁ (pîlegeš).

It refers to a woman in a recognized but generally secondary marital or household relationship, distinct from the standing of a principal wife. The exact legal rights, protections, and circumstances varied across the ancient world.
That distinction matters.
A concubine was not necessarily a prostitute, and the word itself does not prove that every woman so described had been kidnapped, enslaved, or physically forced into the relationship.
But neither does the title establish that she freely consented.
Often, the text simply does not tell us.
And that silence becomes especially troubling when we recognize the unequal power that frequently surrounded these women.
Consider Hagar.
Her story appears in Genesis 16.
She was Egyptian. She was a servant of Sarai. And when Sarai could not conceive, she gave Hagar to Abram in an attempt to obtain children through her.
Genesis 16:3 describes Sarai giving Hagar to Abram "to be his wife" in the King James Version.
The Hebrew uses לְאִשָּׁה (le'ishshah), meaning "as a wife" or "for a wife."

This is important because Hagar is not explicitly called a pîlegeš in that passage. She belongs in this conversation because her story exposes the vulnerability of a woman whose reproductive future was decided within a household where others held authority over her.
We are told what Sarai wanted.
We are told what Abram did.
But Scripture never records Hagar being asked whether she wanted this arrangement.
That does not give us permission to claim we know every detail of her feelings.
It does give us reason to notice whose wishes the narrative records—and whose it does not.
Then Hagar became pregnant.
Conflict followed.
Sarai dealt harshly with her.
And Hagar fled into the wilderness.
Imagine that for a moment.
A pregnant woman, far from her homeland, caught in a family conflict she did not create alone, walking into a dangerous wilderness.
Perhaps she was frightened. Perhaps exhausted. Scripture does not tell us every emotion she felt.
But it tells us something far more important.
God met her there.
Not in a palace.
Not in the center of public attention.
Not where the powerful were making decisions.
In the wilderness.
Genesis 16:13 records Hagar responding to the Lord who spoke to her. The Hebrew includes the extraordinary expression:
אַתָּה אֵל רֳאִי — Attah El Ro'i
Commonly understood as, "You are a God who sees me."
The exact nuance of the Hebrew has been discussed by translators, but the passage unmistakably emphasizes Hagar's encounter with the God who saw her in her distress.
The woman whose wishes were not recorded discovered that heaven had not overlooked her.
And there is something about that which should reach into the deepest places of our own lives.
Because perhaps you know what it means to be useful to people without feeling loved by them.
Perhaps someone valued what you could provide but never considered what their decisions were doing to your heart.
Perhaps you have spent years being strong because no one seemed interested in how much you were hurting.
Hagar's story does not promise that every earthly injustice will disappear immediately.
It reveals something even more foundational.
Being overlooked by human beings does not mean you are invisible to God.
And the Bible does not stop there.
In Genesis 35:22, we meet Bilhah.
Bilhah had been Rachel's servant and became one of Jacob's women through whom he fathered children. Genesis 35 identifies her as Jacob's concubine.
Then, in a brief and devastating report, Scripture tells us that Reuben, Jacob's firstborn, lay with Bilhah.
And Israel heard about it.
That is how abruptly the incident is recorded.
We are not told what Bilhah said.
We are not told whether she resisted, consented, feared retaliation, or was given any opportunity to speak.
We must not declare the incident rape when the passage itself does not provide sufficient detail to establish that conclusion.
But neither should we casually describe it as a consensual affair.
The text does not disclose Bilhah's choice.
Later, Genesis 49:3–4 shows Jacob condemning Reuben's conduct as a grave violation involving his father's bed.
The emphasis falls on Reuben's wrongdoing and its consequences.
But what about Bilhah?
What became of her after the household learned what happened?
Did anyone ask her what she experienced?
We do not know.
And sometimes the most faithful response to Scripture is not to fill its silence with speculation.
It is to acknowledge the silence and refuse to let the person disappear behind it.
Then comes Rizpah.
And if you have never stopped to sit with her story, prepare your heart.
Second Samuel 3:7 identifies Rizpah, daughter of Aiah, as one of Saul's concubines.
After Saul's death, Ish-bosheth accused Abner of having relations with her.
The accusation carried enormous political weight. In the ancient royal world, access to a king's women could signify a claim to royal authority.
Abner responded angrily.
The men argued.
Political alliances shifted.
And Rizpah?
Her own testimony is not recorded.
She appears at the center of a conflict between powerful men, yet we are given no direct account of what she wanted or experienced.
But years later, Scripture brings her before us again.
And this time, we see something extraordinary.
Second Samuel 21 describes seven descendants of Saul being handed over to the Gibeonites and killed during David's reign.
Among them were Rizpah's two sons, Armoni and Mephibosheth.
The passage is morally difficult and deserves careful reading. It must not be turned into a simple model for how justice should be carried out.
But then the narrative gives us one of the most haunting images in the Old Testament.
Rizpah took sackcloth and spread it upon a rock.
And she remained there.
Through the season of harvest.
Through the heat.
Through the nights.
Protecting the bodies from birds and wild animals.
Second Samuel 21:10 records her keeping watch from the beginning of harvest until rain fell from heaven.
We do not know the exact number of days she remained there.
But we know she refused to abandon the dead.
Think about that.
A woman who had been introduced in relation to a king...
A woman whose place in a political conflict had been discussed by men...
Now stood in the open, guarding the remains of her children.
No army.
No throne.
No recorded speech.
Only a mother who would not walk away.
And someone told David what she had done.
The king then arranged for the bones of Saul, Jonathan, and the executed descendants to receive burial.
Rizpah's vigil had become impossible to ignore.
The text does not say that every injustice was corrected.
It does not tell us that Rizpah's grief was healed.
It does not even record her words.
But it makes sure we see her.
Her grief was not given a speech. It was given a place in Scripture.
And perhaps that is why her story still unsettles us.
Because some people do not need another religious explanation for why they should stop grieving.
They need someone to recognize that their grief is real.
Someone to stay.
Someone to care.
Someone who will not treat their suffering as an inconvenience.
And then we come to a woman whose name the Bible never gives us.
The concubine in Judges 19.
This is one of the darkest narratives in all of Scripture.
And it should never be preached casually.
She was associated with a Levite. After a separation, he traveled to bring her back. They eventually stayed in Gibeah, where a violent crowd surrounded the house.
The woman was sent outside.
She was sexually assaulted and abused through the night.
By morning, she was at the doorway.
The Levite told her to get up.
There was no answer.
Judges 19:28, in the King James Version, preserves the chilling words:
"Up, and let us be going. But none answered."

The narrative does not clearly establish the precise moment of her death. What it does establish is that she suffered horrific violence and that her body was subsequently dismembered and used to summon Israel to respond.
The chapter is not a love story.
It is not a justification for treating women as property.
It is a horrifying portrait of moral collapse.
And the wider context of Judges repeatedly emphasizes the disorder of a people who had abandoned righteous judgment.
Judges 21:25 closes the book with this indictment:
"Every man did that which was right in his own eyes."
Notice what happens when people make themselves the final authority over right and wrong.
The vulnerable become expendable.
The powerful justify themselves.
And someone else's body becomes the price of someone else's ambition, anger, or cowardice.
The unnamed woman in Judges 19 never receives a recorded speech.
We cannot know everything she thought.
But we should not need her recorded words to recognize her humanity.
And here is where this story becomes dangerously relevant.
Because the temptation to treat another person as an object did not die in ancient Israel.
It appears whenever someone uses spiritual language to excuse cruelty.
Whenever a leader protects a reputation instead of protecting a victim.
Whenever a family demands silence because the truth might embarrass them.
Whenever a wounded person is told to forgive quickly while the person who harmed them is never called to repentance.
Whenever people care more about preserving power than telling the truth.
And we must say this plainly:
The Gospel never gives anyone permission to exploit another person.
Forgiveness does not make abuse acceptable.
Repentance is not a public-relations strategy.
Grace is not a hiding place for unrepentant wrongdoing.
And submission to God must never be twisted into permission for human cruelty.
The Lord who sees Hagar in the wilderness is not indifferent to what happens behind closed doors.
The God whose Word preserves Rizpah's vigil is not unconcerned with a mother's tears.
And the Scripture that records the horror of Judges 19 is not asking us to admire it.
It is confronting us with the terrible consequences of human sin.
But there is another question we must ask.
What does all of this have to do with Jesus?
Everything.
Because the Bible begins with humanity made in God's image.
Genesis 1:27 declares:
"So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them."
Before there were royal households, concubines, social ranks, or political dynasties, there was this truth.
Human dignity came from God.
Not from marital status.
Not from social power.
Not from wealth.
Not from a man's approval.
Not from a woman's usefulness to somebody else's plans.
From God.
And Jesus Christ did not come to reinforce humanity's sinful habit of assigning value according to power.
He came as the fulfillment of God's redemptive purpose.
Look at the way He treated women in the Gospels.
In John 4, He spoke with a Samaritan woman whose personal history included five husbands and a present relationship with a man who was not her husband.
We must be careful here too.
Jesus did not tell us the reasons behind her five marriages. We cannot responsibly assume she was promiscuous, that she caused every separation, or that she had no responsibility in any of them.
What we know is that Jesus knew her history.
And He still spoke to her about living water.
He revealed Himself to her.
And she went back to her community, telling people about Him.
In John 4:29, she invited them:
"Come, see a man, which told me all things that ever I did: is not this the Christ?"
The woman who came to the well became a witness.
Not because her past was imaginary.
Not because truth no longer mattered.
But because Jesus met her with truth that opened the way to faith.
And then there is the woman in Luke 7 who approached Jesus weeping, wetting His feet with her tears and wiping them with her hair.
Others saw a sinful woman.
Jesus saw her faith, her love, and her response to grace.
He said to her in Luke 7:48:
"Thy sins are forgiven."
And in verse 50:
"Thy faith hath saved thee; go in peace."
The New Testament Greek for "grace" is χάρις (charis).
It carries the sense of favor or gift, and in the theology of salvation it points us toward God's undeserved favor.
Ephesians 2:8–9 says:
"For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast."
Grace is not God pretending sin does not exist.
Grace is God providing salvation through Jesus Christ for sinners who cannot rescue themselves.
At the cross, Jesus did not merely demonstrate sympathy for the wounded.
He bore sin.
He gave Himself for our redemption.
First Peter 2:24 says He "bare our sins in his own body on the tree."
And through His death and resurrection, forgiveness and new life are proclaimed to those who repent and believe.
That is why the Gospel can confront both the person who has been harmed and the person who has caused harm—without confusing their responsibilities.
To the wounded, it declares that their suffering does not erase their dignity.
To the guilty, it declares that repentance is necessary and mercy is available in Christ.
To the proud, it declares that no amount of power can make sin righteous.
To the ashamed, it declares that no past is beyond the reach of God's grace when they turn to Jesus.
And to the church, it declares that we cannot claim to honor Christ while casually disregarding people He commands us to love.
But we must not force every woman in these Old Testament accounts into a tidy redemption story.
Scripture does not tell us that Bilhah received an apology.
It does not tell us that Rizpah enjoyed a peaceful final chapter.
It does not give the unnamed woman in Judges 19 an earthly rescue.
Not every biblical story ends with visible restoration.
And that is precisely why the Christian hope must be bigger than a happy ending in this present life.
Revelation 21:4 looks toward the day when God will wipe away every tear, and death, sorrow, crying, and pain will be no more.
The final answer to evil is not that suffering never mattered.
It is that Jesus Christ, the crucified and risen Lord, will make all things new.
And until that day, His people are called to live differently.
To defend the vulnerable.
To refuse the misuse of power.
To tell the truth.
To repent when we have sinned.
To show compassion without abandoning righteousness.
To seek justice without surrendering mercy.
To remember the people others would rather forget.
Maybe you are reading this because you have spent years feeling like the unnamed person in somebody else's story.
The one who carried the consequences.
The one who was never consulted.
The one whose tears were inconvenient.
The one everyone expected to recover without anyone acknowledging what happened.
I cannot promise you that every person who wronged you will confess.
I cannot promise that your circumstances will change tomorrow.
But I can tell you what Scripture gives us solid ground to believe.
God sees.
God is just.
Jesus Christ is able to save.
And the silence of other people does not determine your worth.
Maybe, instead, this article has exposed something uncomfortable in you.
Perhaps you have used people.
Perhaps you have ignored someone else's suffering because confronting it would have cost you something.
Perhaps you have spoken about holiness while treating another human being without compassion.
Then do not hide behind religious language.
Repent.
Turn to Jesus.
Where you have done wrong, take responsibility. Where possible and appropriate, make restitution. Respect the safety and boundaries of those you have harmed.
Do not demand that someone trust you simply because you say you have changed.
Let repentance produce fruit.
Because the same Gospel that offers forgiveness also calls us into a transformed life.
And maybe this is where the deepest scandal of grace becomes visible.
Jesus does not rewrite everything by pretending the old chapters never happened.
He redeems sinners, creates new life, and promises a final restoration that human power could never accomplish.
The cross does not erase the seriousness of evil.
It shows just how serious sin is—and just how astonishing God's mercy can be.
Not sensationalism for its own sake.
Not outrage without discipleship.
Not emotional stories that leave people moved for five minutes and unchanged afterward.
But Scripture that drives us back to Jesus Christ.
Truth that calls us to repentance.
Grace that leads us toward obedience.
And biblical teaching that helps us recognize the difference between what God commands, what Scripture describes, and what human tradition has sometimes tried to excuse.
Be honest before God.
You do not need to reveal private trauma to prove your faith. Your dignity is not measured by how much you disclose online.
And if God has brought you through a season when you felt invisible, your testimony may encourage someone who is still walking through the wilderness.
And please, do not let this message end with you.
Not simply to increase a number.

But because someone in your circle may have been taught that the Bible excuses the mistreatment of women. Someone may be struggling to reconcile painful experiences with their faith. Someone may need to discover that the God of Scripture sees people whom society overlooks.
Because the goal is not merely to win attention.
It is to point people toward the Savior.
And if you have been blessed by this ministry and want to help us continue, I want to invite you into something deeper.
For those who want to give regularly as an expression of gratitude and worship, this can be one practical way of supporting Gospel ministry.
The New Testament teaches in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not guilt.
Not pressure.
But an opportunity to give freely, according to your means and conviction, toward work you believe glorifies Jesus Christ.
These products can serve as reminders of faith, tools for reflection, and meaningful gifts for others.
It is the opportunity to help the message of Jesus Christ reach another life.
Perhaps another Hagar, feeling unseen.
Another grieving parent who recognizes something of Rizpah's sorrow.
Another person whose story has been defined by decisions they did not make.
Or another sinner who desperately needs to hear that repentance and forgiveness are possible through Christ.
We want these resources to help people read Scripture more faithfully, know Christ more deeply, and grow in spiritual maturity.
Your sharing, thoughtful comments, prayers, and invitations to others also help this work reach further.
You do not have to spend money to glorify God.
You can honor Him by believing His Word, loving your neighbor, caring for the vulnerable, speaking truth, repenting of sin, and faithfully following Jesus wherever He has placed you.
And when you freely choose to support Gospel ministry, that generosity can also become part of your worship.
So before you leave, remember the women we have encountered.
Hagar, seen by God in the wilderness.
Bilhah, whose own account is not preserved.
Rizpah, keeping watch over her sons.
And the unnamed woman in Judges, whose suffering exposes the horror of a society that had abandoned righteousness.
We cannot recover every missing detail of their lives.
We cannot responsibly claim to know every choice they made.
But we can refuse to turn their suffering into entertainment.
We can refuse to confuse biblical description with divine approval.
We can allow these passages to confront our treatment of the vulnerable.
And above all, we can follow the Lord Jesus Christ, who calls sinners to repentance, gives grace to the undeserving, and will one day bring perfect justice and restoration.
Your answer might help someone else read Scripture with greater care and compassion.
Because these women were never merely background characters in the story of powerful men.
They were human beings.
And every time we read their stories with reverence, truth, and compassion, we resist the temptation to overlook the people Scripture has allowed us to see.
The world may remember what happened to you, but in Jesus Christ, what happened to you does not have the final word over who you are.
